newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Signet in radical capital shake-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Signet in radical capital shake-up.

text.p: Signet Group Plc, owner of Ernest Jones and H. Samuel jewellery chains, reported an 80 percent jump in annual profits on Wednesday and proposed a radical shake up of its share capital, including cancellation of dividend arrears.

The long awaited capital restructuring of Signet, the former Ratners jewellery empire, proposes to convert all preference shares into new ordinary shares, and cancels dividend arrears of 164.5 million pounds ($272.2 million).
If approved the plan would give preference shareholders 82.5 percent of the group's new ordinary share capital, and ordinary shareholders stake 17.5 percent, vastly diluting their holding.
But chairman James McAdam was optimistic the proposal stood a good chance of getting shareholder approval.
He said the company's plans to convert all classes of preference shares into new ordinary shares, were pitched at a level which the board considered acceptable to all shareholders.
"This represents what we think will have the best chance of success," McAdam told a news conference.

McAdam said there was no realistic prospect for ordinary shareholders getting any dividends under the existing capital structure. Ordinary shareholders rank behind preference shareholders in terms of receiving dividends.

Investors can vote on the proposal at a meeting scheduled for June 26. Signet has to get 75 percent approval from existing ordinary shareholders and also from 75 percent approval from each class of preference shareholders.

The restructuring, which asks investors to forego 164.5 million pounds in dividend arrears, includes the elimination of a 199 million pound deficit on the firm's profit and loss account. This will pave the way for resumption of dividend payments at some stage, pending court approval.
The chairman said the shake-up increase liquidity in the Signet's shares for all shareholders and take away the debt overhang of unpaid dividends.
McAdam said, however, it was most unlikely the group, which suspended dividend payments in January 1992, would pay a dividend in 1997/98.
Julian Treger of UK Active Value Fund, a Signet preference shareholder which has been pressing for a capital shake-up, said he welcomed the restructuring.
"We've been waiting for a long time for this," he said by telephone, "We welcome it, it will increase the value of the company significantly."

Earlier this year Signet also signed a new three-year credit facility for $360 million with a syndicate of four banks. At the end of the year to February 1 1997 its net debt was 240.2 million stg, down 22 percent.
The group reported 80 percent increase in pretax profits to 45.1 million pounds. Sales were 902.0 billion pounds, up from 894.7 million.
McAdam said this represented a significant recovery from losses of 122 million pounds when he took control of the company in 1992.
"There's still some way to go...but we're getting back to more acceptable levels."

The former Ratners chain, a stock market star in the 1980s under chairman Gerald Ratner, fell on hard times in the early 1990s. The group's troubles started after Ratner made an ill-fated remark at a conference of business leaders rubbishing the retailer's products.
McAdam was brought in to put the company back on its feet. Ratner stepped down and the group eventually changed its name to Signet.
McAdam came under increasing pressure from preference shareholders to restructure the capital, which at one stage included selling off parts of the business.
McAdam said none of the group's businesses were currently up for sale. Last year Signet's UK chains were the subject of an offer from a venture capitalist group, but this was rejected.
The company also owns Kays and Sterling chains in the United States. Its shares closed 5.75 pence lower at 30.75 pence. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
